title.text: Sanctuary of the Sacred Heart of Jesus, Roxas City

title_en.text: Sacred Heart of Jesus Statue (Pueblo de Panay, Roxas City)

tagline.text: A roughly 40 m statue of Christ with open arms on Tumandok Hill, among the tallest of its kind in the Philippines

location.label: Location
location.text: Tumandok Hill inside the Pueblo de Panay development, southern Roxas City, Capiz

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱100~600 (per person, round-trip tricycle from downtown Roxas)

children.text: The Sacred Heart of Jesus statue stands on Tumandok Hill in the Pueblo de Panay development south of Roxas City. The figure is about 31 m tall and about 40 m including its pedestal. It is still an active sanctuary where Mass is held, so it suits pilgrimage, views and a quiet walk alike.

The Sanctuary of the Sacred Heart of Jesus sits atop Tumandok Hill inside Pueblo de Panay, a large mixed-use development in the southern part of Roxas City, the capital of Capiz. The statue of Christ, arms spread wide and looking out over the city and the sea, is the symbol of the sanctuary. English Wikipedia gives the figure's height as about 31 m (102 ft); with its roughly 9 m (30 ft) pedestal the total is about 40 m (130 ft), and it describes the statue as the tallest of its kind in the Philippines. Some local guides give the total height as 132 ft, so the numbers differ slightly depending on whether the pedestal is counted.

The statue is built of reinforced concrete. According to Wikipedia, sculptor John A. Alaban and a seven-man core team led by foreman Jose "Onyot" Clarito, working for Blue Chips Builders, began construction in the last quarter of 2011 and finished on January 5, 2015. A 3 m by 3 m reinforced-concrete core wall supports the figure, with horizontal slabs every 3 m, making it a hollow structure. An interior steel staircase rises to the 8th level, but it is reserved for work crews and closed to the public. The head alone is estimated to weigh 6.5–7 tons and measures 3.8 m from chin to crown. Seen up close, it feels far bigger than it looks in photos.

This is a working sanctuary before it is a sightseeing monument. Pueblo de Panay's own material describes it as a place of prayer, conversion and healing that draws many pilgrims. In December 2019 Typhoon Ursula badly damaged the chapel at the foot of the hill, but the statue remained standing; the Archdiocese of Capiz then began raising funds for a new church and held a groundbreaking on November 7, 2020. The new church was designed by Makati-based BAAD Studio; a 2020 report described it as seating about 920, while a 2022 architecture magazine described pews for 600 plus spill-over space between the buttresses, so the capacity figure varies by source. According to Pueblo de Panay, the developer formally donated the completed sanctuary to the Archdiocese of Capiz on June 7, 2024. Accounts of who commissioned the statue vary by source, so check interior facilities and opening hours on site.

For travelers, this is less a big attraction than a viewpoint and pilgrimage stop that fits neatly into a half-day. It is only about 5 km from the city center, so it combines easily with Roxas City's cathedral and Pan-ay Church in a one-day route. On a clear day the hilltop opens up views over the city, the surrounding fields and the sea. Because it is a religious site, mind your dress and behavior, and be quiet during Mass. Pueblo de Panay is a planned township of about 670 hectares in southern Roxas City, between the Lawaan and Sibaguan highways, and Tumandok Hill is described as about 366 ft (about 110 m) high, so the statue serves as a landmark visible across the development. If this is your first visit to Roxas, seeing the statue before the seafood restaurants or the Panay River promenade is a good way to get a sense of the city's scale. The Capiz Tourism and Cultural Affairs Office is on the 2nd floor of the Provincial Capitol and can be reached at (036) 621-2935 for guides and itinerary questions, while a 2022 news guide lists (036) 651-0585, so sources differ. Contact details may change, so check first.

The sanctuary stands on a hill, so on clear days you see Roxas City, the fields and the sea. Go in the morning or early afternoon, before the sun drops, when the light is soft and the heat is milder.

blocks.title: The atmosphere of a working sanctuary

children.text: This is a pilgrimage site where people come to pray and seek healing. Scheduled Masses, confession and blessings take place, and healing sessions are said to be held on Fridays. Schedules can change, so check before you go.

blocks.title: The statue that survived a typhoon

children.text: In December 2019 Typhoon Ursula badly damaged the chapel at the foot of the hill, yet the statue is said to have stayed standing. Knowing the story that led to the fundraising and groundbreaking for a new church makes the figure look different.

The new church is said to have broken ground in November 2020, and the completed sanctuary was reportedly donated to the Archdiocese in June 2024. Seating is described as anywhere from about 600 to 920 depending on the source; follow the signs on site and check for any work areas or access limits.

Pueblo de Panay is a mixed-use development of about 670 hectares in southern Roxas. The Roxas City Integrated Terminal is also inside the township, so it is easy to add the sanctuary when you arrive or leave.
To fit the whole statue in one frame, step back; up close, a low angle looking up works well. Avoid photographing people at prayer head-on.
Head to the sanctuary by tricycle or taxi from your hotel. Before arrival, tell the driver "Sacred Heart of Jesus Sanctuary on Tumandok Hill" and show the map pin to be sure.
Look up at the statue from its base and take in the view toward downtown and the sea from the viewpoint. In the early hours the sun is less harsh.
Spend a little time inside the sanctuary, respecting the prayerful atmosphere. If the shop is open, you can buy a shawl or souvenirs.
Return downtown and walk the Panay River promenade and Roxas Cathedral.
Roxas is known as the Seafood Capital of the Philippines, so have seafood for lunch.
If you worry about the ride back, ask the driver to wait and agree on a waiting fee in advance.

items.title: Full-day route
items.subtitle: Combining the sanctuary and Pan-ay Church

children.text: Go to the sanctuary early and enjoy the view and prayerful atmosphere.
Hire a tricycle for half a day to see Pan-ay Church and its big bell.
Return downtown and have lunch at a seafood restaurant.
After the heat eases, walk Baybay Beach or the Panay River promenade.
Watch the sunset over the sea to end the day.
Direct flights operate from Manila to Roxas Airport (RXS). Airlines and days change often, so check the latest schedule before booking.
The airport is a short tricycle or taxi ride from downtown. The sanctuary is about
5km
from downtown.
If flights are unavailable or expensive, it is also common to fly into Iloilo or Kalibo and continue overland.
From Iloilo, buses and vans take about
2 hours 30 minutes–3 hours
to reach Roxas. Ceres air-conditioned buses serve the Iloilo–Roxas route.

The Roxas City Integrated Terminal (Pueblo de Panay) is inside the township, so where you get off and the sanctuary are in the same development. Ask at the terminal for the exact distance and how to get there.
Go by tricycle, taxi or private car. It is about 5 km from downtown, so agree on the fare in advance and arrange your ride back too.
"Sacred Heart" alone can be confusing, so say "Tumandok Hill" and "Pueblo de Panay" as well and show the map pin.
December to May, the dry season, is the most comfortable. The hilltop has little shade and strong sun, so go early in the morning or late in the afternoon.

June to November brings frequent rain, and a typhoon crossing northern Panay can change your plans. Typhoon Ursula in 2019 was strong enough to wreck the chapel below the sanctuary, so check weather warnings.

Most hotels cluster around downtown Roxas and Baybay Beach. The sanctuary is close to downtown, so staying in town and taking a tricycle is the easiest way. Pueblo de Panay is a mixed-use development, so you can also grab something simple near the terminal.

For meals, take advantage of Roxas's strength, seafood. Many restaurants and stalls sell oysters, crab, shrimp and shellfish, and prices are lower than in Manila. For items without prices listed, ask for the total before ordering.

It is safer to bring water and snacks from downtown. Having lunch in town and going up in the afternoon helps you avoid the midday heat; if you want a sunset view, work out in advance when you need to come down before dark. There is no confirmed information on night lighting or night opening, so plan on visiting during the day.
Cover your shoulders and knees. According to Pueblo de Panay, shawls are sold cheaply at the Shrine Store, so buy one locally if you did not bring one.
Early morning or late afternoon on a clear day is best for photos and views. Midday is hot with little shade.
Tell the driver "Tumandok Hill" and "Pueblo de Panay" together and show the map pin.
Arrange your ride back in advance. Asking the driver to wait and agreeing on a waiting fee is the surest method.
Keep quiet during Mass and refrain from taking photos. Schedules can change, so check locally.
If you have time, combine it with Pan-ay Church's big bell or Baybay Beach in a one-day itinerary.
Height figures for the sanctuary and statue differ slightly between sources, because guides differ on whether the pedestal is included.
A visit is described as taking about an hour. For pilgrimage, time your visit to Mass; if you only want the view, avoiding Mass times is easier for everyone.
If you need a local guide, contact the Capiz Tourism and Cultural Affairs Office. Contact details may change, so check first.
The staircase inside the statue is for work crews only and off limits, and you must not enter the new church's construction area.
Opening hours and Mass schedules can change often, so check the latest announcement before you visit.
The hilltop has little shade, so midday heat and UV are strong. Bring water and a hat.
In the rainy and typhoon seasons, winds can be strong and paths slippery, so check weather warnings.
During religious services, do not speak loudly or photograph people at prayer.
Agree on taxi and tricycle fares before you ride.
It is a short ride from the sanctuary to downtown. The Panay River promenade, the cathedral and seafood restaurants are clustered there.
East of downtown, Santa Monica Church in Pan-ay has a big bell known as among the largest in Asia. Check locally whether it is open to visitors.
A beach close to downtown that suits watching the sunset. It is better for walking than swimming.
